_meta.author: Eduventure (original questions)
_meta.note: Pre-university and university batch 2: Academic English 8, Research methods 7, Business 8, Environmental science 7, Cybersecurity 6, Artificial intelligence 6, Public health 8. In review until approved in /admin. Contains answers: never imported by src/.

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is most suitable for an academic report?

options.text: The results indicate a significant increase in sales.
The results show sales took a big jump.
Sales went up loads, as you can see.
It's pretty clear stuff sold way more.

questions.explanation: Academic writing uses precise, formal vocabulary (indicate, significant) and avoids slang, contractions and addressing the reader.

wrong.c: "Loads" is slang, and "as you can see" addresses the reader directly.
wrong.d: Contractions (it's) and slang (pretty, stuff, way more) are too informal.

questions.alignment: Academic English for pre-university and first-year study (e.g. MUET / EAP, CEFR B2–C1).

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: What is a thesis statement?

options.text: A sentence that states the main argument of an essay
The list of sources at the end of an essay
A summary of the evidence in each paragraph

questions.explanation: The thesis statement, usually at the end of the introduction, tells the reader the essay's central claim.

wrong.b: That is the reference list or bibliography.
wrong.c: A title names the topic; the thesis states your position on it.
wrong.d: Summaries of evidence belong in body paragraphs or the conclusion.

questions.objective: Recognise the purpose of a thesis statement.
questions.alignment: Academic English: essay writing (e.g. MUET / EAP).

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: Select all the hedging expressions (cautious language) used in academic writing.
questions.explanation: Hedging softens claims to match the strength of the evidence: may suggest, it is possible that, appears to.

wrong.c: "Proves beyond doubt" is a very strong claim, the opposite of hedging.

questions.alignment: Academic English: academic style (e.g. EAP, CEFR B2–C1).

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: Put the parts of a standard academic essay in order.
questions.explanation: Introduction (with thesis) → body paragraphs (arguments and evidence) → conclusion → reference list.
questions.alignment: Academic English: essay writing (e.g. MUET / EAP).

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: True or false: if you paraphrase another author's idea in your own words, you still need to cite them.
questions.explanation: The idea still belongs to the original author. Citing gives them credit and avoids plagiarism, whether you quote or paraphrase.

wrong.false: Changing the words does not make the idea yours: any borrowed idea needs a citation.

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Restating an idea in your own words
Using an author's exact words inside quotation marks
Presenting someone else's work as your own

questions.explanation: Plagiarism is passing off others' work as yours. Paraphrasing and quoting are both acceptable when cited.

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of regular exercise?

options.text: Regular exercise brings several important health benefits.
Some people prefer swimming to running.

questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the paragraph's main idea clearly and covers what the paragraph will discuss.

wrong.b: A personal anecdote is too narrow to introduce the paragraph's main idea.
wrong.c: Preferences between sports are off the topic of benefits.
wrong.d: A single word is not a sentence and makes no point.

questions.alignment: Academic English: paragraph writing (e.g. MUET / EAP).

questions.subject: academic_english
questions.prompt: In APA style, what is the list of all cited sources at the end of a paper called?
questions.explanation: APA uses a "References" list: every source cited in the text appears there, in alphabetical order by author.
questions.alignment: Academic English: referencing (e.g. EAP / APA style).

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: In an experiment, what is the independent variable?

options.text: The variable the researcher deliberately changes
A variable kept the same throughout
An unknown factor that spoils the results

questions.explanation: The independent variable is manipulated by the researcher to see its effect on the dependent variable.

wrong.b: The measured variable is the dependent variable.
wrong.c: Variables kept the same are control variables.
wrong.d: An unwanted factor that affects results is a confounding variable.

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: Which of these is qualitative data?
questions.explanation: Qualitative data describe qualities in words, images or themes rather than numbers.

wrong.b: Reaction times are numerical: quantitative data.
wrong.c: Scores are numerical: quantitative data.

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: True or false: other things being equal, a larger random sample gives a more precise estimate of a population value.
questions.explanation: Sampling error shrinks as the sample grows (the standard error falls with √n), so estimates become more precise. A biased sampling method stays biased, however large.

wrong.false: Random samples vary less from the population value as they get bigger; that is why larger studies give narrower confidence intervals.

questions.objective: Explain the effect of sample size.

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: Select all the features of a randomised controlled trial.

options.text: Participants are randomly allocated to groups
Participants choose which group to join

questions.explanation: Random allocation makes the groups similar, the control group provides a comparison, and outcomes are compared to estimate the effect.

wrong.c: Letting participants choose introduces selection bias; random allocation avoids this.

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: Put the stages of a typical research project in order.
questions.explanation: Question → literature review → data collection → analysis → reporting.

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: Match each sampling method to its description.

right.text: Choosing whoever is easiest to reach
Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
Dividing the population into subgroups and sampling from each

questions.explanation: Random sampling gives everyone an equal chance; stratified sampling ensures each subgroup is represented; convenience sampling is quick but often biased.

questions.subject: research_methods
questions.prompt: In research, what does the reliability of a measure refer to?

options.text: How consistent its results are when repeated
Whether it measures what it is meant to measure
Whether results apply to other settings
Whether the study was ethically approved

questions.explanation: A reliable measure gives similar results under the same conditions, across time or across raters.

wrong.c: That is generalisability (external validity).
wrong.d: That is research ethics, not reliability.

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: In a SWOT analysis, select all the factors that are external to the business.
questions.explanation: Opportunities and threats come from the outside environment (markets, competitors, laws).

wrong.c: Strengths are internal: things the business itself does well.
wrong.d: Weaknesses are internal: things the business itself does poorly.

questions.alignment: Introductory business and management (e.g. diploma / first-year university).

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the original 4 Ps of the marketing mix?
questions.explanation: The 4 Ps are product, price, place and promotion. People was added later in the extended 7 Ps for services.

wrong.b: Product is one of the 4 Ps.
wrong.c: Place (distribution) is one of the 4 Ps.
wrong.d: Promotion is one of the 4 Ps.

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: Fixed costs are RM10,000. Each unit sells for RM25 and has a variable cost of RM15. How many units must be sold to break even?
questions.explanation: Contribution per unit = 25 − 15 = RM10. Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution = 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1,000 units.

mistakes.why: Divide by the contribution (price − variable cost), not the price.
Use the contribution per unit (RM10), not the variable cost.

questions.alignment: Introductory business finance (e.g. diploma / first-year university).

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: A company has revenue of RM200,000 and a net profit of RM30,000. What is its net profit margin, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Net profit margin = net profit ÷ revenue × 100 = 30,000 ÷ 200,000 × 100 = 15%.

mistakes.why: That is revenue ÷ profit; put profit on top.

questions.alignment: Introductory business finance (e.g. diploma / first-year university).

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: True or false: a sole proprietor has unlimited liability for the debts of the business.
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity, so the owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts.

wrong.false: Limited liability comes with forming a company (e.g. Sdn Bhd). A sole proprietor and the business are legally the same person.

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: Match each management function to its description.

right.text: Setting goals and deciding how to reach them

questions.explanation: Planning sets the direction, organising arranges the resources, controlling checks progress and corrects it.

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: Put the stages of the product life cycle in order.
questions.explanation: Introduction (launch), growth (sales rise fast), maturity (sales level off), decline (sales fall).

questions.subject: business
questions.prompt: A car manufacturer buys the company that supplies its tyres. What is this type of growth called?
questions.explanation: Joining with a business at a different stage of the same supply chain is vertical integration. Buying a supplier is backward vertical integration.
questions.alignment: Introductory business strategy (e.g. diploma / first-year university).

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: Which greenhouse gas is released in the largest amounts by burning fossil fuels?
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, the main driver of human-caused global warming.

wrong.b: Oxygen is used up in burning, not released, and it is not a greenhouse gas.
wrong.c: Nitrogen makes up most of the air but is not a greenhouse gas.
wrong.d: Argon is an unreactive gas, not a greenhouse gas.

questions.alignment: Pre-university environmental science (e.g. A-level Environmental Management / foundation).

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: True or false: the ozone layer mainly protects life on Earth from ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation, which can damage DNA.

wrong.false: Ozone's key role is absorbing UV radiation. Its thinning raised skin-cancer risk, leading to the Montreal Protocol.

questions.objective: Explain the role of the ozone layer.
questions.alignment: Pre-university environmental science (e.g. A-level Environmental Management / foundation).

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: Select all the things that can cause eutrophication in rivers and lakes.
questions.explanation: Eutrophication is caused by excess nutrients (nitrates and phosphates), which trigger algal blooms that use up oxygen when they decay.

wrong.c: Riverbank trees help prevent eutrophication by absorbing nutrients and reducing run-off.

questions.alignment: Pre-university environmental science (e.g. A-level Environmental Management / foundation).

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: Put these ecological levels in order, from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: Organism → population (one species) → community (all species) → ecosystem (community plus environment) → biosphere (all ecosystems on Earth).
questions.alignment: Pre-university environmental science / biology (e.g. foundation / A-level).

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: What is the term for the variety of living things in an area?
questions.explanation: Biodiversity includes the variety of species, genes and ecosystems in an area.

wrong.b: Biomass is the total mass of living material.
wrong.c: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area.
wrong.d: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support.

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: Match each pollutant to its main environmental effect.
questions.explanation: CFCs break down ozone; sulphur dioxide dissolves in rain to form acids; carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere.

questions.subject: environmental_science
questions.prompt: Producers in a food chain store 10,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy (in kJ) passes to the primary consumers?
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat, movement and waste. 10% of 10,000 = 1,000 kJ.

mistakes.why: 100 kJ would reach the secondary consumers, two levels up.
9,000 kJ is the energy lost, not the energy passed on.

questions.objective: Calculate energy transfer between trophic levels.
questions.alignment: Pre-university environmental science / biology (e.g. foundation / A-level).

questions.subject: cybersecurity
questions.prompt: What is phishing?

options.text: Tricking people into revealing information through fake messages or websites
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment

questions.explanation: Phishing uses messages that pretend to come from trusted sources to steal passwords, card numbers or other data.

wrong.c: That is a denial-of-service attack.

questions.subject: cybersecurity
questions.prompt: Select all the good security practices for accounts.

options.text: Sharing your password with a trusted friend

questions.explanation: Password managers make unique, strong passwords practical, and two-factor authentication protects accounts even if a password leaks.

wrong.c: If one site is breached, a reused password unlocks all your other accounts.
wrong.d: Passwords should never be shared; anyone who has it can act as you.

questions.subject: cybersecurity
questions.prompt: True or false: HTTPS encrypts the data sent between your browser and the website.
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt traffic, so others on the network cannot read or change it. It does not prove the website itself is honest.

wrong.false: The S stands for secure: HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS encryption.

questions.subject: cybersecurity
questions.prompt: Match each attack to its description.

right.text: Flooding a service with traffic from many machines
Inserting malicious database commands through input fields

questions.explanation: Ransomware holds data hostage; DDoS overwhelms a service; SQL injection abuses unchecked input to run database commands.

questions.subject: cybersecurity
questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of two-factor authentication?

options.text: A password plus a code sent to your phone
A password plus a security question

questions.explanation: Two-factor authentication combines different kinds of factor: something you know (password) and something you have (your phone).

wrong.b: Both are something you know, so this is one factor used twice.
wrong.c: A username is not secret; only the password is a factor.
wrong.d: Both are something you know: still a single factor type.

questions.subject: cybersecurity
questions.prompt: What is the security principle of giving each user only the access they need to do their job?
questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege limits the damage if an account is misused or compromised.

questions.subject: artificial_intelligence
questions.prompt: Which type of machine learning learns from examples that are labelled with the correct answers?
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on input–output pairs, such as photos labelled "cat" or "dog".

wrong.b: Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data.
wrong.c: Reinforcement learning learns from rewards gained by acting in an environment.
wrong.d: Clustering is an unsupervised technique: it groups unlabelled data.

questions.alignment: Introduction to AI and machine learning (e.g. second-year university).

questions.subject: artificial_intelligence
questions.prompt: True or false: overfitting means a model performs well on its training data but poorly on new data.
questions.explanation: An overfitted model has learned noise and quirks of the training set instead of the general pattern, so it does not generalise.

wrong.false: That is exactly overfitting. Doing poorly on both training and new data is underfitting.

questions.alignment: Introduction to machine learning (e.g. second-year university).

questions.subject: artificial_intelligence
questions.prompt: Match each task to the type of machine learning problem.

left.text: Labelling emails as spam or not spam
Grouping customers by behaviour, with no labels

questions.explanation: Regression predicts numbers, classification predicts categories, and clustering finds groups without labels.
questions.alignment: Introduction to machine learning (e.g. second-year university).

questions.subject: artificial_intelligence
questions.prompt: Select all the techniques that help reduce overfitting.

options.text: Adding many more parameters to the model

questions.explanation: More data, regularisation (penalising complexity) and early stopping (halting before the model memorises the training set) all improve generalisation.

wrong.c: More parameters make a model more flexible, which usually increases overfitting.

questions.alignment: Introduction to machine learning (e.g. second-year university).

questions.subject: artificial_intelligence
questions.prompt: In reinforcement learning, what does an agent learn from?

options.text: Rewards and penalties from its environment

questions.explanation: The agent tries actions, receives rewards or penalties, and learns a policy that maximises long-term reward.

wrong.b: Labelled examples are used in supervised learning.
wrong.c: Clustering unlabelled data is unsupervised learning.
wrong.d: Hand-written rules describe classic expert systems, not learning.

questions.subject: artificial_intelligence
questions.prompt: A classifier labels 120 test examples and gets 90 right. What is its accuracy, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Accuracy = correct ÷ total × 100 = 90 ÷ 120 × 100 = 75%.

mistakes.why: 25% is the error rate (30 wrong out of 120).

questions.alignment: Introduction to machine learning (e.g. second-year university).

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: What is herd immunity?

options.text: Indirect protection of people who are not immune, because most of the population is
Immunity that animals give to humans
Immunity a person is born with
Immunity that lasts for life after one infection

questions.explanation: When enough people are immune, a disease cannot spread easily, which protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns.

wrong.b: Herd immunity is about population-level protection, not animals.
wrong.c: That is innate immunity.
wrong.d: Lifelong immunity in one person is individual immunity, not herd immunity.

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: A person weighs 70 kg and is 1.75 m tall. What is their body mass index (BMI), to one decimal place?

mistakes.why: Divide by height squared, not height: 70 ÷ 1.75 = 40.

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: True or false: antibiotics are effective against viral infections such as the common cold.
questions.explanation: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses. Using them for colds does not help and contributes to antibiotic resistance.

wrong.true: Viruses lack the structures antibiotics target. Colds and flu are viral, so antibiotics do not treat them.

questions.objective: Explain the appropriate use of antibiotics.

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: Select all the modifiable risk factors for heart disease.
questions.explanation: Modifiable risk factors are ones a person can change: smoking, activity level and diet.

wrong.c: Age cannot be changed: it is a non-modifiable risk factor.
wrong.d: Family history cannot be changed: it is non-modifiable.

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: Match each disease to how it mainly spreads.
questions.explanation: Dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes, cholera by contaminated water or food, and influenza by droplets from coughs and sneezes.
questions.alignment: Introductory public health and epidemiology (e.g. first-year university).

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: In epidemiology, what does incidence measure?

options.text: The number of new cases in a population over a period
The total number of existing cases at one time
The number of deaths from a disease
The number of people who recovered

questions.explanation: Incidence counts new cases over time, showing how fast a disease is spreading.

wrong.b: That is prevalence: all current cases, new and old.
wrong.c: Deaths are measured by mortality.
wrong.d: Recoveries are not what incidence measures.

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: Put the steps of washing your hands in order.

options.text: Scrub all surfaces for at least 20 seconds

questions.explanation: Wet, soap, scrub for at least 20 seconds, rinse, dry. Scrubbing long enough is what removes most germs.

questions.subject: public_health
questions.prompt: What is the term for a disease outbreak that spreads across several countries or continents, affecting many people?
questions.explanation: A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread internationally, such as COVID-19.
